_comment: Hand-written benchmark answers for the evaluator (Milestone 5). Each case names a bank question by its exact text prefix and an expected label. 'expect' holds the bounds that answer should satisfy. Labels: strong, partial, incorrect, irrelevant, keyword_stuffed, paraphrase, concise_correct, unsupported. These are synthetic practice answers written by the developers, not real candidate data, and agreement on them is not proof of real-world accuracy.

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Overfitting is when a model learns the noise in the training data, so it scores very well on training data but poorly on new data. I detect it by comparing training and validation performance, for example a training accuracy of 99% against 80% on validation, and by using cross-validation and learning curves. To prevent it I add regularization such as L2 or dropout, use early stopping, simplify the model or collect more data, and I keep a separate test set that is only used for the final check.

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: Overfitting means the model memorises the training data and then does badly on new data. You can notice it when the training score is much higher than the validation score. I usually just try a smaller model when that happens.

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Overfitting means the model is too simple, so it cannot learn the patterns in the training data. More training accuracy always means a better model, so the fix is to add more layers and train for many more epochs until the training loss is zero.

cases.q: What is overfitting

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: A model overfits when it memorises quirks of its training set, so it looks great there but fails on unseen data. I spot it when the held-out score is much worse than the training score, using k-fold checks and learning curves. To avoid it I use weight decay or dropout, stop training once the validation loss starts rising, and keep a final test set untouched until the end.

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: Overfitting is when a model fits noise in the training data and generalises poorly. I detect it with a gap between training and validation scores using cross-validation, and prevent it with regularization, early stopping and a separate test set.

cases.q: What is overfitting
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: Overfitting is never a real problem if you use a big enough neural network. Deep learning always generalises, everyone in industry knows this. Just trust the model and ship it.

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: First I would stop looking at accuracy, because with 1% positives a model that predicts the majority class gets 99%. I use precision and recall, F1 or PR-AUC instead. I make a stratified split so both sets keep the class ratio. Then I try class weights in the loss, resampling such as random oversampling or SMOTE on the training set only, and finally I tune the decision threshold based on the cost of false negatives versus false positives. In a churn project this raised recall from 0.42 to 0.71.

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: I would oversample the minority class so both classes have similar counts, and then train the model as usual. I would also check the confusion matrix to see how it does on the small class.

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Accuracy is the best metric for imbalanced data because it summarises everything in one number. I would oversample the whole dataset before splitting into train and test so the test set is also balanced, which makes the results look better.

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: irrelevant

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: keyword_stuffed

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: When one class is rare I don't trust the share of correct predictions; I look at how many flagged cases are right and how many real cases we catch, plus the area under the precision-recall curve. I keep the class ratio the same in every split, give the rare class a bigger penalty in the loss, create synthetic minority examples only on the training data, and move the cut-off for a positive prediction to match the business cost of each mistake.

cases.q: How would you handle an imbalanced dataset
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: I would use precision and recall instead of accuracy, keep a stratified split, apply class weights or SMOTE on the training data only, and tune the decision threshold to the business cost.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: Imbalance doesn't matter for modern models. XGBoost always handles it perfectly by itself, so there is nothing you need to do. It is the best approach, trust me.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Bias is error from a model that is too simple, which underfits, and variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training data, which overfits. As model complexity grows, bias falls and variance rises, so validation error first goes down and then up. For example, a linear model on a curved relationship has high bias, while a very deep decision tree has high variance. I pick the complexity with the lowest validation error and use regularization or ensembles like bagging to reduce variance.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: Bias is when the model is too simple and variance is when it is too complex. You want something in the middle. A decision tree can have high variance.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: High bias means the model overfits the training data and high variance means it underfits. Adding more complexity always reduces both bias and variance, so the deepest model is always the best choice.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: irrelevant
cases.answer: My favourite programming language is Python because the syntax is clean and there are many libraries for web development and automation scripts that I use at home.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: keyword_stuffed
cases.answer: Bias, variance, underfitting, overfitting, model complexity, validation error, regularization, ensembles, bagging, trade-off.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: A model that is too rigid misses real structure in the data, so it is wrong in a systematic way even on training data. A model that is too flexible chases noise, so its predictions swing a lot with each new sample. Making the model more flexible removes the first problem but adds the second, so the held-out error is U-shaped. For example, a straight line on curved data is too rigid, and a very deep tree is too flexible; I choose the point where held-out error is lowest and use penalties or averaging many models to calm the flexible ones.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: Bias is underfitting from a too-simple model and variance is overfitting from a too-complex one. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance, so I choose the complexity with the lowest validation error and use regularization or ensembles.

cases.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: The trade-off is a myth from old textbooks. Modern deep models always beat it and never overfit, it is obvious if you have worked in the industry.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Fraud is rare, so accuracy is misleading: predicting no fraud gives 99.8%. I would report precision and recall, and PR-AUC as the threshold-free summary because ROC-AUC looks optimistic on rare classes. The decision threshold comes from business cost: a missed fraud might cost 500 dollars while a false alarm costs a short manual review. Because fraud patterns change, I validate with a time-based split, training on older months and testing on the latest month.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: I would use precision and recall because fraud is rare. Recall is important so we catch most fraud cases.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Accuracy is the best metric for fraud detection because it is easy for the business to understand. I would use a random split of all transactions and pick the model with the highest accuracy, which will be about 99%.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: keyword_stuffed
cases.answer: Fraud, accuracy, precision, recall, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC, threshold, business cost, time-based validation, F1.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: Since almost every transaction is legitimate, the share of correct predictions tells us nothing. I care about how many alerts are really fraud and how many fraud cases we catch, summarised by the area under the precision-recall curve. Where to cut the score depends on money: a missed fraud costs far more than one analyst check. I also test on the most recent weeks after training on earlier ones, because fraudsters change tactics.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: Accuracy is misleading because fraud is rare, so I use precision, recall and PR-AUC, set the threshold from the business cost of errors, and validate with a time-based split.

cases.q: Which evaluation metrics would you choose for a fraud detection model
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: The only metric that matters is AUC, always. Every serious company uses it and nothing else, so no other analysis is needed.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Most indexes are B-tree structures that keep column values sorted with pointers to rows, so the database can find matching rows in logarithmic time instead of a full table scan. They help most on selective columns, such as an email column, and much less on a low-selectivity column like a boolean. They hurt writes, because every insert and update must also update each index, and they use storage. I check whether a query uses an index with EXPLAIN and the query plan before and after adding it; on one table this took a lookup from 900 ms to 4 ms.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: An index is like the index of a book, it helps the database find rows faster. You should add indexes on columns you search often.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Indexes always make queries faster and they have no cost, so you should add an index on every column of every table. They also speed up inserts because the data is already organised.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: irrelevant
cases.answer: I started learning guitar last year. I practise thirty minutes every evening and I can now play a few songs for my friends.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: keyword_stuffed
cases.answer: B-tree, index, full table scan, selectivity, slower writes, EXPLAIN, query plan, storage, primary key, composite index.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: An index is a separate sorted tree of a column's values that points to the rows, so the engine can jump to the right rows instead of reading the whole table. It pays off when a value narrows the result to a few rows and much less when a column has only a couple of distinct values. Every insert, update or delete must also maintain the tree, so writes get slower and it takes disk space. I confirm the engine actually uses it by reading the execution plan before and after.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: An index is usually a B-tree that avoids a full table scan; it helps selective columns but makes writes slower, and I verify it with EXPLAIN on the query plan.

cases.q: How do database indexes work
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: Indexes are basically magic. Just index everything and performance problems disappear, that is what every senior engineer does.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: A transaction groups several operations so they succeed or fail together, all or nothing. ACID means atomicity, the all or nothing part; consistency, so constraints like a non-negative balance always hold; isolation, so concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work, with isolation levels such as read committed or serializable; and durability, so committed data survives a crash because it is written to the log. For example, a bank transfer debits one account and credits another in one transaction, so money is never lost if the server fails halfway.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: A transaction is a group of SQL statements that run together. ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. It makes the database reliable.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: A transaction is just a single SQL query. Atomicity means each query runs very fast, and durability means the data stays in memory so it can be read quickly. Isolation is not important for web applications.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: irrelevant
cases.answer: During my free time I watch documentaries about space, especially about Mars missions and how rockets are launched.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: keyword_stuffed
cases.answer: Transaction, atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, ACID, commit, rollback, isolation levels, constraints, bank transfer.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: A transaction bundles several changes so either every change is saved or none is. The guarantees are: the bundle is indivisible; rules such as foreign keys and checks still hold afterwards; transactions running at the same time don't see each other's half-finished changes, with stronger or weaker settings for that; and once saved, the change survives a power cut because it is in the write-ahead log. Moving money between two accounts is the classic example.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: A transaction is all or nothing; ACID means atomicity, consistency with constraints, isolation between concurrent transactions via isolation levels, and durability after commit, for example a bank transfer.

cases.q: What are database transactions
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: Transactions are outdated; modern databases never need them and everyone uses NoSQL now, so ACID does not matter at all.

cases.q: How do authentication and authorization differ
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Authentication checks who you are, for example a login with email and a password stored as a bcrypt or scrypt hash. Authorization checks what you are allowed to do, such as whether this user may edit this order. Both must be enforced on the server for every request, because the client can be modified; I never trust a role or user id sent by the browser. For example, the API returns 404 if user A requests user B's interview, even though user A is logged in.

cases.q: How do authentication and authorization differ
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: Authentication is logging in and authorization is permissions. Both are important for security in web apps.

cases.q: How do authentication and authorization differ
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Authentication and authorization are the same thing, they both mean logging in. It is fine to hide admin buttons in the frontend because users cannot change the JavaScript, and storing passwords in plain text is acceptable for small apps.

cases.q: How do authentication and authorization differ
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: The first step proves identity: the user signs in and we compare a salted hash of the password, never the raw password. The second step decides access: can this signed-in person open or change this particular resource. Both decisions happen in backend code on every request, since anything coming from the browser can be forged; for example, another user's record is answered with not found.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: JavaScript runs on a single thread with one call stack. When an async operation like a timer or fetch finishes, its callback is put in a queue. The event loop takes work from the queues only when the stack is empty, and it runs all microtasks, such as promise callbacks, before the next task like a setTimeout callback. The browser can render between tasks, so a long synchronous loop blocks clicks and painting; I avoid blocking by splitting work or moving it to a web worker.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: JavaScript is single-threaded, and async code like setTimeout runs later through the event loop. Promises also run later.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: JavaScript is multi-threaded, so every setTimeout callback runs in parallel on its own thread. A setTimeout with 0 ms always runs before any promise callback, and long loops never block the page.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: irrelevant

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: keyword_stuffed
cases.answer: Event loop, single thread, call stack, callback queue, microtasks, tasks, promises, setTimeout, rendering, blocking, web worker.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: Only one piece of script runs at a time on the main thread, tracked by a stack of function calls. Finished timers, network responses and clicks leave callbacks waiting in lines. When the stack is empty, the loop first drains all promise continuations, then takes one waiting callback such as a timer, and the browser may repaint between those turns. That is why a heavy synchronous computation freezes the page; I break it into chunks or hand it to a worker.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: concise_correct
cases.answer: JavaScript has a single thread and call stack; callbacks wait in queues, microtasks run before the next task, the browser renders between tasks, so I avoid blocking the main thread.

cases.q: Explain how the browser event loop
cases.label: unsupported
cases.answer: The event loop is not something developers need to understand, frameworks always hide it completely, so it never matters in practice.

cases.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: In a university project, a teammate wanted to store all data in MongoDB while I believed PostgreSQL fitted our relational data better. Instead of arguing in the group chat, I asked for a short call, listened to his reasons, which were mainly speed of setup, and then I built a small prototype of both and measured query complexity for our three main reports. The evidence showed joins were central, so we agreed on PostgreSQL and I helped him set it up. The project was delivered on time, and I learned that data and listening resolve disagreements faster than opinions.
